n: Safely ashore, the survivors learned they had landed on Malta, an island south of Sicily.
The islanders showed remarkable kindness, building a fire and welcoming everyone out of the cold rain. “Barbarous” simply means they didn’t speak Greek — not that they were savage.

f.g: Non-Greek-speaking people; the Maltese spoke a Punic (Phoenician) dialect.

n: As Paul helped gather firewood — the great apostle doing humble work — a snake driven out by the heat bit his hand.
The islanders concluded Paul must be a murderer: he escaped the sea, but Justice (perhaps a goddess they revered) would not let him live.

f.g: Greek Dikē — “Justice,” personified as a goddess who punishes the guilty.

n: Paul simply shook the snake into the fire and suffered no harm — fulfilling Jesus’ promise to his disciples.
They waited for him to swell up or drop dead. When nothing happened, they swung to the other extreme and decided he was a god — as happened at Lystra.

f.w: said that he was a god

n: Nearby was the estate of Publius, the island’s chief official, who hospitably hosted them for three days.

f.w: the chief man of the island
f.g: An official title — “first man” of Malta — confirmed by inscriptions found there.

n: Publius’s father was ill with fever and dysentery. Paul prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him — repaying kindness with a priesthood blessing.

f.w: laid his hands on him, and healed him

n: Word spread, and the other sick people on the island came and were healed.
The grateful islanders honored them in many ways and, when they left, supplied everything they needed for the journey.
After three winter months, they sailed on another Alexandrian ship with the twin gods Castor and Pollux as its figurehead — patrons of sailors.

f.g: The “Twin Brothers” of Greek myth, sons of Zeus, believed to protect sailors.

n: They stopped at Syracuse, the main city of Sicily, for three days.

f.g: A major port on the east coast of Sicily.

n: Sailing on, they reached Rhegium at the toe of Italy, then with a south wind arrived at Puteoli, a key port near Naples.

f.g: Modern Pozzuoli, near Naples — a major port for Alexandrian grain ships.

n: At Puteoli they found fellow believers who invited them to stay a week. Then they set out for Rome.

f.g: Members of the Church — the gospel had already reached Italy.

n: Believers from Rome walked out to meet Paul at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns, about 40 and 30 miles from the city. Seeing them, Paul thanked God and was encouraged.

f.g: Market of Appius, a stop on the Appian Way about 43 miles from Rome.

n: In Rome, Paul was allowed to live in his own lodging, guarded by a single soldier — a mild form of custody.
Three days later Paul called together the Jewish leaders of Rome. He explained he had done nothing against his people or their customs, yet had been handed over to the Romans.
The Romans had examined him and wanted to release him, since he had done nothing deserving death.
When the Jewish leaders objected, he was forced to appeal to Caesar — not to accuse his own nation.
That’s why he invited them — he wears this chain because of “the hope of Israel”: the Messiah and the resurrection.
They replied that they had received no letters or bad reports about him from Judea.
But they wanted to hear his views, since this “sect” was spoken against everywhere.
On an appointed day, many came to his lodging. From morning to evening he explained the kingdom of God and tried to persuade them about Jesus from the law of Moses and the prophets.

f.w: out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets

n: Some were persuaded; others refused to believe — the familiar response throughout Acts.
As they left disagreeing, Paul had one final word, quoting what the Holy Ghost spoke through Isaiah.
Isaiah’s commission: these people will hear but not understand, look but not see. Hearing without a willing heart doesn’t lead to understanding.

f.w: Hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand

n: Their hearts have grown dull and they have shut their eyes and ears — otherwise they would turn and be healed. God longs to heal; people close themselves off.
Therefore, God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles — and they will listen. This fulfills the pattern of Acts: from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

f.w: the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles

n: The Jewish leaders left, arguing intensely among themselves. Many ancient manuscripts omit this verse.
Paul lived two full years in a rented house, welcoming everyone who came. During this house arrest he likely wrote letters such as Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon.

f.g: Rented lodging; Paul likely paid his own costs.

n: Acts ends not with Paul’s death but with the gospel going forward boldly and unhindered in the capital of the world. The story of the Church continues — and invites us into it.

f.w: with all confidence, no man forbidding him
f.g: The final Greek word, akōlytōs, means “unhindered.”
